Take caution in using LLMs as human surrogates | PNAS

# Take caution in using LLMs as human surrogates

Yuan Gao https://orcid.org/0009-0005-9433-1242 yuangg@bu.edu, Dokyun Lee https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3186-3349, Gordon Burtch https://orcid.org/0000-0001-9798-1113, and Sina Fazelpour Authors Info & Affiliations

Edited by Susan Fiske, Princeton University, Jamaica, VT; received January 23, 2025; accepted May 9, 2025

## Significance

This paper critically evaluates the potential dangers of employing large language models (LLMs) as surrogates for human participants or as simulations of human behavior in social science research. Through an in-depth empirical case study, we find that LLMs do not exhibit behavior consistent with humans in a simple scenario. Further, LLMs demonstrate inconsistent and idiosyncratic responses. We explore failure modes, analyze their limitations from empirical and philosophical perspectives, and propose practical guidelines for future research. Our study underscores the importance of transparency and rigor to ensure replicable and reliable research in this emerging area.

## Abstract

Recent studies suggest large language models (LLMs) can generate human-like responses, aligning with human behavior in economic experiments, surveys, and political discourse. This has led many to propose that LLMs can be used as surrogates or simulations for humans in social science research. However, LLMs differ fundamentally from humans, relying on probabilistic patterns, absent the embodied experiences or survival objectives that shape human cognition. We assess the reasoning depth of LLMs using the 11-20 money request game. Nearly all advanced approaches fail to replicate human behavior distributions across many models. The causes of failure are diverse and unpredictable, relating to input language, roles, safeguarding, and more. These results warrant caution in using LLMs as surrogates or for simulating human behavior in research.

Recent studies report that Large Language Models (LLMs) can exhibit human-like cognitive abilities. These studies demonstrate that LLMs produce outputs that closely resemble responses from human subjects in seminal experiments from behavioral economics and responses comparable to those of humans in perceptual tasks and standard theory of mind (ToM) evaluations (1– 3). Early work in this area (4) suggests that LLMs generate outputs consistent with human preferences and biases in decision-making and behavior more generally, across a variety of domains, including economics (1), political science (5), marketing (6), and psychology (7– 9).

On this basis, studies claim that LLMs may serve as useful surrogates or simulation testbeds for human subjects in social science research (10– 12), an idea that has also gained traction in industry, e.g., for market research (6). * For example, the startup Synthetic Users † employs LLMs to simulate consumer reactions to new products. The benefits of using LLMs as human surrogates have been argued from several perspectives, including cost-effectiveness, scalability (13), and the idea that LLMs can provide synthetic data in cases where they have traditionally been scarce (1).

The growing enthusiasm for using LLMs as human surrogates in research raises two urgent questions for the scientific community. First, do findings demonstrating LLMs’ capability as surrogates for human participants generalize to less explored or newer research contexts? Second, to what extent are LLMs’ outputs subject to configuration and implementation choices? To the extent the outputs of LLMs do depend on such choices, we argue they require careful documentation and evaluation by researchers and reviewers invested in ideals of replicable and responsible science (14– 16). This work investigates these issues.

We begin with an empirical case study demonstrating that several LLMs are incapable of serving as faithful human surrogates in a simple experiment, wherein we show that the models’ generated outputs systematically and significantly diverge from those of human participants. Our experiment utilizes the 11–20 money request game (17), a simple economic game designed to evaluate participants’ depth of strategic reasoning. ‡ We begin by exploring variation in responses to the experiment instructions across eight popular LLMs (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude3-Opus, Claude3-Sonnet, Llama3-70b, Llama3-8b, Llama2-13b, and Llama2-7b). We collect responses from 1,000 clean sessions for each LLM and compare the distribution of those responses to the distribution of previously reported human participant responses and Nash Equilibrium predictions. We demonstrate that the LLMs’ outputs differ markedly from those of human participants. Moreover, we show significant variation in response distributions across LLMs. Notably, the most recent and largest models do not necessarily generate more human-like responses, a finding that runs counter to the notion that more human-like responses may be induced or enabled in LLMs through scaling (18). And, comparing LLMs’ responses with those of humans across game variants specifically designed to elicit certain reasoning modes, we find that the changes in LLMs’ outputs these variants induce differ from those exhibited by human participants; LLMs are generally less sensitive to changes in game design.

Next, we extend the experiment by applying three advanced techniques that have been proposed to enhance LLM performance in reasoning. Broadly, we demonstrate that regardless of the approach used, LLMs generate unstable outputs that differ from human behavior to a statistically significant degree. Specifically, our analysis reveals a few key findings. First, all approaches involving tests with out-of-distribution (OOD) examples § consistently fail to elicit human-like outputs, regardless of the LLM used. Second, providing explicit human behavioral examples as part of prompting via Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) or fine-tuning makes LLM output distributions slightly more similar to those of human participants. Surprisingly, however, none of these approaches is fully capable of inducing behavior that replicates human-like distributions across the studied LLMs, with the sole exception of a fine-tuned GPT-4o. Even then, because the fine-tuning process was implemented using examples of human responses that were documented in the paper that first introduced the 11-20 money request game, we believe the fine-tuned GPT-4o is merely mimicking the provided examples, and its ostensibly human-like response is thus limited to the specific patterns and contexts it has encountered. This explanation is further reinforced through experiments involving Centaur (19), a newly released fine-tuned model based on Llama 3.1, which was trained on extensive human data with the explicit goal of emulating human behavior. Despite this, Centaur, like the other LLMs we consider, fails to replicate human behavioral patterns in our game.

We further show that LLMs’ responses vary significantly based on the provision of in-context examples during prompting, as well as with changes in prompt framing, even when the game instructions remain unchanged. For example, instructions to respond “rationally” versus “like a human” lead to different output distributions, as does changing the prompt language (English, Chinese, Spanish, or German). This underscores the instability of LLM outputs and the issue of prompt brittleness.

Having established the divergence of LLMs from human-like behavior and the instability of their output in a simple setting, we next examine LLMs’ self-explanations, provided alongside their numeric game responses, to better understand LLMs’ failure modes. ¶ We identify numerous inconsistencies in the self-explanations. We observe discrepancies between the explanations provided by LLMs and their actual outputs. Additionally, we observe that some advanced models produce outputs inconsistent with or incorrect relative to the game instructions, despite the simplicity of the task. Here, it should be noted that Arad and Rubinstein’s discussion of human participants’ self-explanations made no mention of any apparent inconsistencies between those explanations and game choices, nor was it observed that human participants’ explanations ever contradicted the game instructions (17). These findings indicate that LLMs’ self-explanations are unreliable, and caution should be exercised when using them as indicators of the models’ internal reasoning processes. The findings also indicate, again, that LLMs’ outputs differ markedly from that of humans in this game.

We then consider the degree to which models’ responses may depend on their prior memorization of the experiment and past findings. Whereas the various LLMs appear incapable of providing the instructions associated with the experimental game we consider here (an indicator that the game has not been memorized by these models), each is generally perfect at recalling the instructions associated with classic economic games that evaluate the same level-k reasoning abilities, games for which prior work has reported that LLMs’ tend to perform in a very human-like manner (20– 22). This observation, along with LLMs’ divergence from human samples’ response distributions and failure in OOD scenarios in the 11-20 money request game, suggests the potential role of memorization as a driver of LLMs’ previously documented ability to simulate human-like behavior in certain experiments.

We contextualize our findings within the broader discussion of LLM failure modes, which may arise from the inherent differences between LLM objective functions—focused on memorizing and predicting the statistical regularities of online textual data—and human objective functions—centered on survival and reproduction—as discussed in the literature on the philosophy of AI (23, 24). We provide an overview of recent empirical research on LLMs that relates to our findings, highlighting LLMs’ inherent flaws, such as performance inconsistency, reliance on memorization, and prompt brittleness, all of which significantly limit the feasibility of using LLMs in studying human behavior or as human surrogates.

Finally, drawing on these experiments and emerging explanations, we turn to our second question of critically examining the methodological choices and assumptions inherent in deploying LLMs as human surrogates-from experimental design to interpretation-and highlighting key considerations that warrant careful documentation. In doing so, we take care to delineate valid use cases of LLMs, scenarios in which integrating human behavioral data into LLM workflows is beneficial, from problematic use cases, particularly scenarios where LLMs serve directly as surrogates or as simulations for studying human behavior, absent any sort of validation against data from humans. Building on our empirical findings, we also formulate targeted questions and criteria to guide rigorous implementation and evaluation in valid use cases.

## LLMs Fail in a Simple Experiment

### 11-20 Money Request Game and Level-k Reasoning.

Level-k thinking is a theoretical framework used in game theory and behavioral economics to model strategic decision-making in interactive settings (25). It suggests that individuals operate at varying reasoning levels and base their strategies on iterative predictions about others’ reasoning depth. This framework is particularly effective for analyzing real-world strategic interactions where perfect rationality and complete information are unrealistic. Empirical evidence indicates that Level-k models often accurately reflect human behavior in experimental settings (26). Under this framework, prior studies have demonstrated that LLMs generate responses indicative of reasoning depth comparable or superior to that of humans in the classic beauty contest game (20– 22).
